title: Lunch aboard Mikasa: supply and illness behind the blockade
dek: A menu from 30 May 1904 connects life aboard a Japanese warship with the work of its supply ships. The episode is described in Akinori Ishihara’s 2024 study.

sections.title: A day aboard ship
paragraphs: Rice and barley, miso soup with dried daikon and tea for breakfast; stewed canned salmon with hijiki seaweed for lunch. This was Mikasa’s menu for 30 May 1904, as reported by researcher Akinori Ishihara in his article on Japanese naval supply. A list of provisions brings everyday life aboard ship into the history of the Port Arthur blockade—a side of the war easily lost among accounts of combat operations.

According to Ishihara, after taking part in blockade operations, Mikasa underwent maintenance from 10 May at a forward base among the islands south of Liaodong. The story of this lunch takes place there, outside Port Arthur harbour.

sections.title: 156 people fell ill after lunch
paragraphs: Ishihara links 156 cases of food poisoning aboard Mikasa to the canned salmon served at this lunch: it had spoiled after exceeding its storage life. In his article, the menu becomes part of the fleet’s medical history.

Food poisoning also occurred aboard other Japanese ships in May and June 1904, Ishihara writes. The records he cites mention canned goods, spoiled food and mouldy bread. In some cases the cause could not be established. He also notes the efforts made aboard Mikasa to serve cooked food.

sections.title: The fleet needed supply ships
paragraphs: Delivering and storing food formed part of a wider task. According to Ishihara’s study, two supply ships initially served the fleet: Matsuyama Maru and Fukuoka Maru. The plan called for supplies to reach the forward bases roughly every six days. Two ships proved insufficient for a fleet operating in dispersed groups. Kotohira Maru joined them in August 1904; other vessels were also used, although they lacked adequate food-storage facilities.

The blockade is usually seen from Port Arthur: Russian ships inside the harbour, Japanese ships outside. Lunch aboard Mikasa adds another scale to this picture. A ship taking part in the blockade itself needed maintenance and safe food. Repeated, routine tasks made its operations at sea possible. Ishihara’s study traces them through food deliveries and an occasion when an ordinary meal left many people ill.

limitations: This account draws on Ishihara’s 2024 article, rather than a direct reading of the original medical volume. The source he lists is 極秘 明治37.8年海戦史, Part 7, 医務衛生, Volume 7; NIDS reference ⑨その他－千代田-536.
156 is the number of food-poisoning cases aboard Mikasa, not deaths or losses across the fleet. Any comparison with hunger or mortality in besieged Port Arthur would require other evidence.

Maintenance does not establish that the ship was undergoing repairs for battle damage. No causal link has been established between the shortage of supply ships and the spoilage of this particular batch of canned salmon.

The menu of 30 May 1904 is distinct from the combat rations served at the Battle of Tsushima on 27 May 1905, discussed in the same article. The modern article’s illustrations and prepared table are not reproduced here.

sources.title: Ship Logistics During the Russo-Japanese War: Rice Balls Were Served for a Post-Victory Dinner
sources.author: Akinori Ishihara (石原明徳), National Institute for Defense Studies, Japan
sources.locator: NIDS Commentary, No. 324. Pages 7–8; note 13 on page 10. Printed page numbers match the PDF page numbers.
sources.note: Original title: 日露戦争における艦のロジスティクス―勝ち戦の夕食は握飯. A modern study based on naval documents. The menu, food-poisoning episode and supply ships are described with attribution to the author; the original medical volume has not been checked separately.

title: Dairen’s money through the eyes of a bank clerk
dek: In Sun Yaoting’s later recollections, the history of money unfolds through banks, different means of payment and the difficulty of obtaining a loan.

sections.title: A bank on Tianjin Street
paragraphs: Sun Yaoting left an address in his memoir that offers a starting point for the history of money in Dairen: Tianjin Street, as it was called when he wrote. Here, he says, stood the joint Japanese-Chinese Longkou Bank where he worked. His account of the city’s banking life comes from someone who knew it from the inside.

Sun writes that he had lived in Dalian since childhood and entered banking in 1930. He recalls his work, changes at banks and mergers, and his progress from apprentice and clerk to senior positions. A broad discussion of urban finance thus acquires a particular vantage point: working experience inside a bank office.

His account of the city’s Japanese period later appeared in the second issue of Materials on the History of Dalian. Sun sees the city from within banking circles: institutions and means of payment sit alongside the question of the borrower’s position.

sections.title: The name of a currency does not explain a transaction
paragraphs: In Sun Yaoting’s account, different means of payment circulated in the city. He describes Japanese banknotes, calling them jinpiao (金票), silver money and paper issues from Chinese banks. Even this list makes it difficult to reduce Dairen’s monetary life to a single sum without specifying the currency and period.

The institutions issuing money also occupied different positions. According to Sun, issues by local Chinese banks depended on permission from the Japanese authorities and served as temporary means of payment. He describes the predominance of Japanese banknotes. Alongside the question of what people paid with comes another: who was allowed to issue money, and on what terms?

The term jinpiao needs care. It refers to banknotes and cannot simply be translated as gold coins. To examine a particular purchase or loan, we would need to establish the currency issue, date and terms of acceptance. The memoir supplies names and distinctions from which that investigation can begin.

sections.title: Who could borrow?
paragraphs: When Sun Yaoting turns to credit, monetary history becomes a question of access. In his recollection, an ordinary person found it difficult to obtain a bank loan. Borrowing from a bank or money house required adequate collateral. He writes about traditional private credit firms, qianzhuang (钱庄), and separately about usurious lending outside these institutions. What mattered to a borrower was whether the money could be obtained at all, and on what repayment terms.

This is testimony from someone familiar with banking, but his generalisations cannot automatically be treated as statistics for the whole city. The text uses anticolonial and class-based judgements; Japanese financial institutions are presented as instruments of exploitation. That language also reveals the author’s position and how he later understood his experience.

Sun Yaoting’s memoir helps us ask a more precise question about Dairen’s money. Before converting an old sum into modern rubles, we need to establish when the transaction took place, which money was used and what choices its participants had. For that inquiry, the bank clerk left us an occupation, an address and a set of institutions.

limitations: Pages 49–53 of the library PDF were used. The article continues beyond this extract; no claim is made to have read it in full. The publication date of the collection’s second issue has not been established.
A later personal account does not represent all Chinese residents of Dalian. The author’s generalisations about currency circulation and lending need to be checked against bank reports and contracts.

Interest rates are not given: the units of calculation, loan periods and terms in the checked extract could not be established with sufficient confidence. The conditions described for the Japanese period are not applied to Russian Dalny at the start of the century or to Russian prices in 1913.
Tianjin Street is described as current at the time the memoir was written; its present-day name has not been checked separately. The exact building and whether it survives have not been established.
